title: API Inspector Training in the Northeast & Mid-Atlantic
description: API 510, 570, 580 and 653 exam prep for inspectors at Delaware River refineries, New York Harbor terminals and Mid-Atlantic plants, studied online.
h1: API inspector training for the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic: Delaware River refining, harbor terminals and the pipelines between them
html:
Inspection work between the Chesapeake and New York Harbor looks different from the Gulf Coast. There are fewer refineries, and several of the plants that once refined crude now store, process or ship other products. What the region has in abundance is tankage: terminal after terminal along the Arthur Kill, the Kill Van Kull and the tidal Delaware, fed by the long products pipelines from the south. That mix makes API 653 unusually valuable here, keeps API 510 and API 570 in demand at the remaining refineries and gas-liquids plants, and puts a premium on knowing how New Jersey and Pennsylvania layer their own rules on top of the API codes. This page explains where those jobs are, how state law changes the way an API code is applied, and how a candidate in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland or northern Virginia can prepare with Atlantis's self-paced online course.

Refining that remains on the Delaware River

Three refining sites remain on the river between Philadelphia and Delaware Bay, and a fourth refinery sits in Linden on New York Harbor.

  • Trainer, Pennsylvania. Monroe Energy, a Delta Air Lines subsidiary since 2012, runs the Trainer refinery about fifteen miles south-west of Philadelphia, at about 190,000 barrels per calendar day in EIA's 2026 refinery survey, with a large share of its output turned to jet fuel.
  • Paulsboro, New Jersey, and Delaware City, Delaware. PBF Energy owns both, and EIA's 2026 survey lists Paulsboro at 160,000 and Delaware City at 171,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation capacity. The two plants are about 30 miles apart and PBF runs them in combination to handle a wide variety of crude oils.
  • Linden, New Jersey. Phillips 66's Bayway refinery stands on the Elizabeth border inside the Port of New York and New Jersey and is described as the northernmost refinery on the US East Coast.

Two other sites show how much the region has changed. Upstream at Marcus Hook, the former Sunoco refinery that shut in 2011 was rebuilt by Energy Transfer as a terminal for processing, storing and loading natural gas liquids onto ships, supplied mainly by the Mariner East pipelines. In South and Southwest Philadelphia, the 1,300-acre former refinery site is now the Bellwether District, where HRP Group is building warehouses and manufacturing space. For an inspector, plants in second lives raise exactly the questions the API codes handle: what changed when the service changed, which equipment was rerated, and which old records still describe the metal truthfully.

New York Harbor and the products pipelines: API 653 country

The harbor is a storage market first. Kinder Morgan's Carteret terminal alone covers 197 acres on the Arthur Kill with 280 tanks between 2,000 and 260,000 barrels, about 8.9 million barrels of capacity, six ship and barge docks, and pipeline connections to the Colonial and Buckeye systems. Its tanks hold petroleum products, ultra-low sulfur diesel, ethanol, biodiesel and chemicals. Its Perth Amboy terminal, also on the Arthur Kill, lists 113 tanks and about 3.5 million barrels for biofuels, chemicals and petroleum, and its Philadelphia terminal on the Delaware lists 100 tanks for chemicals and ethanol. Other operators run more tankage along the New Jersey shore and the river.

The supply arrives by water and by pipe. Colonial Pipeline describes its system as about 5,500 miles of line running from Houston to Linden, with one mainline carrying gasoline and another distillates, a line into New York Harbor and another ending in central Maryland. Terminal tanks that switch between gasoline grades, distillates, ethanol and biodiesel give an inspector more to think about than a crude tank that holds one product for decades: API RP 571 describes ethanol stress corrosion cracking, for example, and a change of service is one of the triggers API 653 tells you to assess.

Atlantis's New York Harbor RBI page goes further into terminal damage mechanisms, and the guide to API 653 inspection intervals covers the interval rules the exam asks about.

State tank rules that change how API 653 is applied

An inspector who studies API 653 in this region also has to know where state law narrows the code. Two state rules stand out.

StateRuleWhat it means for an API 653 inspector
New JerseyN.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16(d), field-erected steel tanks of more than 2,000 gallons at regulated facilitiesAtmospheric tanks follow API 653 and its schedule, but API 653's similar-service and risk-based inspection scheduling are not permitted. Pressure tanks follow API 510 or ASME Section VIII, and API 510's similar-service and risk-based scheduling are excluded too.
PennsylvaniaChapter 245 aboveground tank inspections, administered by the Department of Environmental ProtectionTanks over 5,000 gallons, and highly hazardous substance tanks over 1,100 gallons, need periodic inspections: in service within five years of installation and then at most every five years, and out of service for tanks over 21,000 gallons within ten years of a new tank or bottom and then at most every twenty years. Inspections must be performed by DEP-certified inspectors in the IAM or IAF category.

Two consequences follow. First, an API 653 certificate does not make you a Pennsylvania-certified tank inspector; the IAF certification for field-constructed tanks is a separate state credential. Second, much of what API 653 says about risk-based intervals cannot be used to schedule regulated tanks at New Jersey facilities, even though you still need to know it for the exam and for terminals elsewhere. Atlantis's pages on API 653 work in New Jersey and API 653 work in Pennsylvania describe both regimes from the owner's side.

Pressure vessel jurisdictions and owner-user inspectors

For API 510 candidates the state boiler and pressure vessel laws matter just as much.

New Jersey's Mechanical Inspection Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance, part of the Department of Labor and Workforce Development, has overseen boilers and pressure vessels since 1913, and its own figures put unfired pressure vessels at roughly three for every boiler. The bureau makes the first inspection of new equipment; after that the owner may use the state or an authorized insurance-company inspector, or run an in-house programme as an Owner-User Inspection Organization under N.J.A.C. 12:90-3.19, with certificates of competency for its inspectors.

Pennsylvania's Boiler and Unfired Pressure Vessel Law, Act 104 of 2013, sets inspection of unfired pressure vessels every 36 months. Inspections are made by Commonwealth inspectors or commissioned insurance inspectors, a Pennsylvania commission requires a National Board commission card, and an owner can have its own employees commissioned to inspect boilers and vessels used in process operations.

So a Northeast owner-user inspector often carries two kinds of credential: the API certificate that shows command of the inspection code, and the state commission or certificate of competency that allows them to inspect for the jurisdiction. The exam-prep course is aimed at the API certificate and does not cover the state credential.

Gas liquids, LNG and Mid-Atlantic piping

South of the Delaware, the large inspection sites are less about crude. Cove Point LNG, near Lusby on the western shore of the Chesapeake in Calvert County, Maryland, is operated by BHE GT&S and has exported LNG since its export project was completed in early 2018. The Kinder Morgan-operated Plantation pipeline runs up from Baton Rouge to the Washington area, with an extension from Richmond to Alexandria, Virginia, and Colonial's fourth line ends in central Maryland. Along those routes sit products terminals with their own tanks and piping.

At gas-liquids plants and LNG sites the work is mostly API 510 and API 570: pressure storage, process vessels, cryogenic and pressurised piping. Note one boundary that candidates sometimes blur. API 653 covers aboveground atmospheric tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C. Pressurised spheres and bullets for propane or butane are pressure vessels, so they belong to API 510, and refrigerated LNG storage tanks are built to standards such as API 620 and API 625 rather than API 650, so API 653 is not their core document.

A worked API 570 example from gas-liquids service

API 570 sorts piping into classes by the consequence of a leak, and services that can vaporise rapidly on release, such as propane, fall into Class 1. Say a propane line read 0.300 inch four years ago and reads 0.280 inch now, and its required thickness is 0.200 inch. The short-term corrosion rate is 0.020 divided by 4, or 0.005 inch a year. The remaining life is 0.080 divided by 0.005, or 16 years, so half the remaining life is 8 years. API 570's recommended maximum thickness-measurement interval for Class 1 piping is 5 years, so the next thickness readings are due within 5 years, the smaller of the two figures. The same line in Class 2 service would have a 10-year class maximum and the interval would be set at 8 years by the remaining-life limit instead. Practise questions built this way, where the class limit and the remaining-life limit compete, until picking the governing figure is automatic.

Studying for an API exam from a Northeast job

Many Northeast inspectors work for contractors on rotating site assignments, commute long distances or come through union apprenticeships. Atlantis's course is self-paced and online for that reason: there are no class times to keep, you can study on a train or after a night shift, and an instructor answers your questions as you work through the codes. Some habits that suit the region:

  • Study the code your employer's sites actually use first. A harbor terminal inspector will absorb API 653 and API 650 faster than a candidate who has never stood on a tank floor, and that confidence carries into the harder clauses.
  • Separate state rules from the exam. The New Jersey and Pennsylvania rules above shape your working life but are not examined; when you practise, answer strictly from the API code and the documents on your window's effectivity sheet.
  • Practise the open-book half on screen. During the exam the codes are provided as PDFs on the computer, so get used to searching and navigating them rather than flipping printed pages.

API 510, API 570 and API 653 are sat in person at Prometric test centres, and Prometric's test-centre locator shows the sites nearest your home or work. API's scheduling page lists API 580 as available through remote proctoring. Seats are allocated first-come, first-served within your window, and API's exam schedule page sets out how windows and deadlines work.

Who qualifies, and through which route

API, not Atlantis, decides eligibility and issues certification. API 510, API 570 and API 653 each combine education with experience gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency: one year for an engineering or technology degree, two for a two-year degree or certificate, three for a high-school diploma and five or more with no formal education, with at least one year of supervising or performing inspection on the longer routes. In the Northeast the common routes are tank and NDT technicians at terminal inspection contractors, refinery and plant maintenance staff moving into owner-user inspection, union pipefitters and boilermakers with repair and construction experience, and engineers in integrity groups. API 580 is automatic for holders of a current 510, 570 or 653 certificate. Details are on the API 510, API 570 and API 653 certification pages.

Sponsoring candidates across a terminal network

Terminal operators with sites in several states often sponsor a group of inspectors in the same year. Because each candidate works to their own timetable, inspectors in Carteret, Philadelphia and Baltimore can start at different times and still share one enquiry and one quote. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually, sits the exam individually and receives an individual result. Atlantis also offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training in the region, with pages for Philadelphia, Newark, New York, Baltimore and Pittsburgh, and AWS CWI exam prep with pages for Philadelphia, Newark and Baltimore.

faq.q: Does an API 653 certificate make me a Pennsylvania DEP-certified tank inspector?
faq.a: No. Pennsylvania requires its periodic aboveground tank inspections to be performed by individuals certified by the Department of Environmental Protection, in the IAM category for manufactured tanks or the IAF category for field-constructed tanks. API 653 certification is a separate credential issued by API. Many Pennsylvania tank inspectors hold both, and the API course does not prepare you for the DEP certification.

faq.q: Can a New Jersey terminal use API 653 risk-based inspection to set its tank intervals?
faq.a: For field-erected tanks of more than 2,000 gallons covered by N.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16(d), the rule requires API 653 to be followed but does not permit its similar-service or risk-based inspection scheduling. A risk assessment can still help rank tanks and target inspections within the required schedule. API 580 and API 653 candidates still need to know the RBI provisions for the exam.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia, Newark or Baltimore?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia, Newark, Baltimore or anywhere else in the Northeast; Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. The API exam-prep courses are studied online at your own pace with instructor Q&A, and the examinations are sat at Prometric test centres, or remotely for API 580 where API allows it.

faq.q: I inspect tanks and transfer piping at a harbor terminal. Should I take API 653 or API 570 first?
faq.a: Many terminal inspectors start with API 653, because shells, bottoms, roofs and foundations are where the regulated inspections and the big repair decisions sit. API 570 then covers the manifolds, dock lines and transfer piping. If your employer's piping programme is the bigger gap, the order can reverse. The comparison of which certification to take first sets out the trade-offs.

faq.q: Are propane spheres covered by API 653 or API 510?
faq.a: API 653 covers atmospheric storage tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C. Pressurised spheres and bullets for propane, butane or other gas liquids are pressure vessels, so their in-service inspection falls under API 510, along with the state pressure vessel law. That boundary matters at Marcus Hook-style gas-liquids terminals and at refineries with LPG storage.

faq.q: Does the course teach the New Jersey and Pennsylvania state rules?
faq.a: The course is built on API's Body of Knowledge and the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your exam window, because that is what the examination tests. State rules such as New Jersey's discharge prevention regulations and Pennsylvania's Chapter 245 are not on the API exams. This page summarises them so you can see how they sit beside the code in practice.

faq.q: Can union members or contractor employees enrol without employer sponsorship?
faq.a: Yes. Individuals can enrol on their own, and the self-paced format lets you study between site assignments. Before enrolling, check that your experience will meet API's eligibility rules for the code you want, because API, not Atlantis, decides whether your application is accepted and the course does not change that decision.

faq.q: How do I choose an exam window?
faq.a: Each API examination runs in set windows during the year, and each window has an application deadline. Choose a window that leaves enough study time after any turnaround or outage you are committed to, then apply to API before the deadline. Atlantis keeps the current windows and deadlines on its API exam schedule page.
